children.text:
For your product to be fit for purpose, it has to be able to automate your customer's ability to switch to a competing product with little to no friction.

This is a really great identification of why, from an investing perspective, AI is nothing like past technologies.

> I see that all the money is being invested in AI and data centers but I do not quite understand why.

I am no economist or business person but AFAICT the massive amount of money being burned is because everyone in the space believes there will be a Google-like (for search) single winner who takes all when the dust settles on the AI race.

Because of this belief they are willing to burn any amount of money they can get their hands on to get to this mythical finish line as fast as they possibly can, seeing it as existential. Moving fast (particularly when your main cost is hardware capex) means moving expensively.

The real question is why anyone (let alone everyone) believes this single-winner theory in 2026 when all available evidence over the past few years shows that there is neither a moat nor a lock-in opportunity at all in this market.

For your product to be fit for purpose, it has to be able to automate your customer's ability to switch to a competing product with little to no friction. And all of the competing products are roughly the same in capabilities over a long enough timeline. Good luck building any kind of real moat with that burden.

But I guess after a certain point after you've taken on hundreds of billions of dollars of investment you're pot committed and just have to keep going through the motions even if you later see the futility, perhaps that's where the AI labs are now...? Either that or just common variety denial.

This, to me, is the most interesting question in all of this. I increasingly feel like we live in a 'post-truth' world with regards to money and the stock market in particular. The fed, and government alike, seem to have gradually shifted their mandates from trying to provide to a stable playground to trying to create a playground where important kids are never allowed to fall down. And when your existence is tied to trillions of dollars of the economy, you become the important kid.

Come to think of it this is also probably being exasperated by the rise of money management firms controlling tens of trillions of dollars. When the market valuation is technically just based on sentiment and you control that much money in a self-interested way, you're going to get weird outcomes.

There's a finite amount of training data available, and multiple companies have downloaded all of it. Arguably, trying to get a monopoly on training data is equivalent to getting monopoly access to the open internet + books.

That ain't going to happen, and if it somehow did in the US, things like Anna's Archive + libgen will save the rest of the planet from our self-imposed dark ages.

As for those data centers: The cost of inference and training on the same hardware is dropping much faster than Moore's Law. That multiplies with hardware advances, since Moore's Law isn't quite done yet.

So, those datacenters are depreciating at 50% every 18 months (Moore's law) at the same time as performance/$ and performance/watt of the software is dropping at some crazy rate like 10x per year. So, token per unit of data center is increasing by something like > 20x every 18 months, and that'll probably happen at least one more time. If it does, the datacenters will be provisioned to produce 400x more tokens than they could have when they were sized.

Put another way, if the singularity is coming, the first things it will destroy are those data center build outs. That doesn't matter though: the data centers are being built on circular loans, so the money needed to complete them probably never existed.

Dark times ahead; hopefully Trump will be blamed, since all this corruption happened on his watch while he had control of the senate, house and (partially) the courts. The stock-goes-down graph will show it happening after the midterms, of course.

children.text: Nah there's plenty of TAM for frontier models even if just to take over market share from cheaper models. Fields like law or medical cn always use lower hallucination rates and smarter "human social" intelligence.

Conversely, the TAM for tasks that cheap models can and have been able to one-shot for a while now is orders of magnitude larger than the TAM at the frontier. While it’s kind of cool that frontier models are able to solve Millennium Prize problems, there just isn’t a huge market for that sort of thing. Otherwise, professional mathematicians would be getting paid a lot more than they do now, and there would be more of them.

Chess is a fixed target, so as a benchmark, it can be saturated.

Reality can’t be saturated. The set of things you can accomplish with more intelligence is unbounded. So while cheap models will continue to proliferate, there will always be a massive market at the frontier, and that won’t ever change.

Here's why I'm skeptical:

It may only be a short-term circumstance that you need a data centre to run AI for lucrative applications. Thirty years ago you needed a mainframe to beat Kaspersky at chess. Algorithm's got better, and now you can beat the mainframe that beat Kaspersky with a bot running on a desktop Pentium of the day[1]. You could still, today, devote a full hyperscale data centre to create a chess bot to beat all other chess bots, but nobody is doing that because there's no money in it.

The frontier is continually pushed outwards. At it's outer edge you need mainframes and data-centres. Once it pushes past, you don't. There wasn't a lot of money in Chess or protein folding, despite the later having huge potential for public benefit. There is a lot of money in coding and middle management, and that's what currently has tech-bros in a frenzy. However, there's no guarantee that what the frontier moves onto next will be lucrative. It might be more chess and protein folding. If, as Algorithm's and hardware improve, coding moves to local models (Sam Altman's nightmare) and nothing lucrative immediately replaces that, what are these companies going do do with their massive data-centres?

The scale of investment we're seeing these companies commit only makes sense if they have multiple decades to reap the returns. They may well not have that much time.

children.text:
> As an imaginary example, I wouldn't be shocked if some company like Jane Street is secretly investing a billion dollars to create the highly specialized synthetic RLVR data needed to train an AI that gives them an average .08% edge on a certain kind of commodity, equity or asset trade.

The crazy thing is ... it's not imaginary, nor is secret, it's literally a video on YouTube from five months ago - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8J-GUnfSqeE (though that facility is only showing of ~$200 million worth of compute).

> would be like an expensive Bloomberg Terminal or an investment letter that offers valuable and expensive intelligence.

Whether it's Anthropic or not, I think it's inevitable some highly specialized offerings will emerge. I suspect there are already some incredibly sophisticated, hyper-narrow, astronomically expensive models being created for private in-house use.

As an imaginary example, I wouldn't be shocked if some company like Jane Street is secretly investing a billion dollars to create the highly specialized synthetic RLVR data needed to train an AI that gives them an average .08% edge on a certain kind of commodity, equity or asset trade. If so, it's not a leap to imagine another company spending $100M on a model that gives a .008% edge and selling access to 100 high-volume institutional traders for $2M each.

Expanding general purpose LLMs to incorporate increasingly specific use cases has, so far, seemed to be economically viable but I don't see a fundamental reason that must remain true for incredibly narrow yet ultra high-value domains requiring monumental bespoke development, data, etc to profitably exploit.

children.author: dofm
children.text:
I assume some of this is the escalating cost of training, indeed, and that being faster means abandoning efficiency.

But you’re right. I have often wondered why it is that such a small amount of extra compute (300MW) from SpaceX was entirely enough for them to uncap so many customers.

I think the (in-house) data centre burdens of ever-more complex models may be considerable, but I think the data centre businesses expecting to serve inference tasks are probably heading into a Chinese real estate bubble.

What always confuses me about Anthropic is them insisting that they need more compute.

This feels wrong in several ways:

a) they're certainly not addressing their customers like they're compute-limited. One must ask, what would that look like? For one, I think it'd look like a wait list to sign up. It'd look like prices going _higher_, and not lower

b) IIUC, their revenues don't cover their _current_ compute costs. So, let's pretend coreweave magics up a new dc and hands it over to anthropic, which means presumably anthropic needs to start paying for it. How does that affect anthropic's revenue? AFAICT, it just adds costs, it doesn't make their revenue go up.

The only interpretation I can find is if Anthropic is _convinced_ that they need to train faster/harder, and that doing so would somehow significantly shift their TAM or costs, for example by coming up with a model that was simply 10+ years ahead of anyone else that costs the same as opus 5.5 to run, and they instantly nab the entirety of openai's market share. Seems pretty unlikely.
